newsitem.title: USA: NHL ICE HOCKEY-WHALERS REJECT NEW STADIUM PROPOSAL AND WILL MOVE.
newsitem.headline: NHL ICE HOCKEY-WHALERS REJECT NEW STADIUM PROPOSAL AND WILL MOVE.

text.p: The Hartford Whalers have agreed to pay $20. 5 million to escape the final year of their lease with the Hartford Civic Centre and then the NHL team will relocate in time for next season.
"The Hartford Whalers will be leaving Connecticut at the end of this season," Whalers' owner Peter Karmanos said on Wednesday.

"We will be working closely with the league to determine where the team will relocate. We have not yet taken any steps in that regard as our efforts, to date, have been focused on trying to stay in Connecticut."

Connecticut Governor John G. Rowland earlier announced the breakdown in negotiations with the team to keep it in Hartford, saying, "I can report to you that the Whalers ... will agree to pay the state a total of $20.5 million as their exit fee,"

Rowland said the Whalers would not agree to a long-term lease of 20 years or more. He said Karmanos wanted the state to cover the proposed $45 million in losses that the team would incur in the three years waiting for a new building.

"It would be very difficult for me to go to the legislature and propose a $147 million arena without a long-term agreement from the Hartford Whalers," Rowland said. "Our hands were tied. Mr. Karmanos obviously believes that there's a better deal out there, otherwise we would have been in a much better negotiating position."
"We regret when circumstances force any team to relocate," said NHL Commissioner Gary Bettman. "We recognise and appreciate the support the Whalers have received during their time in Hartford."
With the $20.5 million payment and the projected losses for this season, Karmanos said the team will have lost $91 million in three years.
The Whalers also wanted a new facility rent-free. The state offered a $2.5 million per-year rent. Karmanos also wanted committments by May 1st for luxury suites and pledges for 13,000 season tickets.

"We've had a good run for the last 17 or 18 years," Rowland said. "Mr. Karmanos and the Whalers ownership have made a business decision. We've made a decision, I believe, that is in the best interest of the Hartford community and in the best interests of the tax payers of this state.
Columbus, Ohio and St. Paul, Minnesota provide possible relocation options, as does Nashville, Tennessee, which nearly lured away the New Jersey Devils during that team's 1995 run to the Stanley Cup.

The Whalers entered the NHL in 1979 as one of four teams absorbed from the defunct World Hockey Association. They were a charter member of the WHA and won the league's first title in after the 1972-73 season.
The Whalers, in 10th place in Eastern Conference, have not made the playoffs since 1992.

The Whalers are averaging 13,570 fans per game in 36 home dates this season and have not had a crowd under 11,000 after having nine under the figure last season. Capacity at the Civic Centre is 15,635.
